query: Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys have reported densities of 1.46–6 g/cm3 and commonly contain solid solutions together with intermetallic compounds. Earlier induction-melted Al–Mg-rich alloys established this structural complexity but did not resolve subsequent transformation pathways. Compositionally graded MgAlCuZnGd alloys showed region-dependent compression and corrosion performance, while studies of AlMgₓTiSnZn alloys associated Mg content with phase stability and multiple functional properties. Most prior work emphasized hardness and room-temperature compression, leaving corrosion, high-temperature oxidation, and evolution from metastable states comparatively underexplored. Within the design constraint of density below 6 g/cm3 and the tendency for constituent-property differences to promote stable intermetallic compounds, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain how a non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy evolves and why that evolution changes its corrosion and high-temperature oxidation behavior? Specify an unnamed controlled comparison, predictions relative to the initial baseline, boundary conditions, supporting prior observations, and an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A nanocrystalline Mg-containing HEA produced via high-energy ball milling followed by spark plasma sintering, when subjected to a mild aging treatment at 300°C for 1 hour, will develop coherent grain-boundary intermetallic precipitates that block intergranular corrosion pathways and provide preferential sites for forming a dense, protective oxide film during high-temperature exposure, thus enhancing both corrosion and oxidation resistance.
generation.material_initial_state: Nanocrystalline Mg-containing HEA synthesized through ball milling and SPS, with a predominantly metastable single-phase structure and high density of grain boundaries.
generation.intervention: Post-consolidation aging at 300°C for 1 hour in an inert atmosphere.
generation.conditions: Aging under inert atmosphere to prevent premature oxidation, followed by corrosion tests in a chloride medium and oxidation tests at elevated temperatures (e.g., 700°C in air).
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of coherent intermetallic precipitates along grain boundaries.
generation.mechanism: Grain-boundary precipitates interrupt continuous corrosion pathways, reduce galvanic differences at grain interfaces, and promote nucleation of a uniform, adherent oxide scale at high temperatures.
generation.predicted_outcome: An anticipated improvement of approximately 25% in oxidation resistance (slower scale growth) and a decrease in corrosion propagation rates relative to a non-aged SPS sample.
generation.baseline: Nanocrystalline HEA produced by ball milling and SPS without any aging treatment.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies for aging treatments around 300°C for ~1 hour; significantly different aging temperatures or durations could lead to over-coarsening or phase instability.
generation.uncertainty: The exact kinetics of grain-boundary precipitation may vary with slight compositional variations and processing parameters, possibly affecting the magnitude of improvement.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize nanocrystalline HEA powders via ball milling and consolidate by SPS. Divide samples into two groups: one to receive an aging treatment at 300°C for 1 hour and one as the control. Conduct microstructural characterization (TEM, grain-boundary analysis), followed by corrosion tests in 0.1 M NaCl and oxidation tests at 700°C.
measurements: Oxide scale thickness and morphology (via SEM)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the aged samples do not exhibit a significant increase in grain-boundary precipitates and corresponding improvements in corrosion and oxidation resistance compared to the control, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The aim of the present work is to investigate the influence of systematic variations in Mg content on the microstructure, mechanical properties, and corrosion behavior of these alloys. By characterizing the resulting intermetallic phases, grain refinement, and passive film formation, this study identified how processing and composition synergistically affect the corrosion resistance and mechanical performance. This work offers new insights into the design of corrosion-resistant, high-strength materials and represents a novel extension of compositionally complex alloy design to Mg-rich systems.

This study investigated the effects of composition and processing on the microstructure, hardness, elastic modulus, and corrosion resistance of spark plasma sintered Mg-Ti-Zn alloys. Key findings include: MgTiZn and Mg4TiZn alloys were produced via ball milling and spark plasma sintering. XRD, SEM, and STEM analyses revealed the presence of multiple phases. Both TZ and 4TZ exhibited high hardness and stiffness, which were much higher than those of any commercial Mg alloy. Both TZ and 4TZ exhibited high corrosion resistance (indicated by the high corrosion potential and low corrosion current density) and passivation, which were attributed to the formation of a Ti rich surface film. These findings demonstrate the potential of combining mechanical alloying and SPS to engineer Mg-containing multi-principal element alloys with a rare combination of high hardness and corrosion resistance. This strategy offers a new pathway for designing lightweight structural or biomedical materials that overcome the traditional strength–corrosion trade-off in Mg and Zn alloys. papers.title: Modeling and Experimental Results of Selected Lightweight Complex Concentrated Alloys, before and after Heat Treatment.
papers.approach: Non-equilibrium solidification simulations (CALPHAD, kinetic and diffusion‐driven precipitation simulations) combined with induction melting and heat treatment experiments
papers.findings: Observed multiphase microstructures comprising a dominant solid-solution phase accompanied by intermetallic compounds (e.g., Mg2Si, Al9Mn2Si). Two invariant transformations were noted in one alloy system with phase stability windows (e.g., BCC-A2 stable between 316–488 °C) and differences in precipitation sequence between alloys.
papers.mechanism: Diffusion-driven precipitation from a non-equilibrium solidified state leads to the sequential formation of intermetallic phases from an initially supersaturated solid solution.

papers.title: Microstructure, Phase Formation and Heat-Treating of Novel Cast Al-Mg-Zn-Cu-Si Lightweight Complex Concentrated Aluminum Based Alloy.
papers.approach: Casting (gravity permanent mold) and heat treatment combined with CALPHAD-based phase diagram analysis
papers.findings: The alloy exhibited a multiphase microstructure featuring a major α-Al matrix with reinforcing intermetallic phases. Precipitation transformations from as-cast metastable states to equilibrium phases were correlated with changes in mechanical performance.
papers.mechanism: A non-equilibrium as-cast structure evolves during heat treatment via controlled precipitation, modifying the distribution and nature of intermetallic phases that influence subsequent oxidation and corrosion responses.

papers.title: Corrosion Behavior of MgTiZn and Mg4TiZn Alloys After Ball Milling and Subsequent Spark Plasma Sintering.
papers.approach: High-energy ball milling (mechanical alloying) followed by spark plasma sintering (SPS) and subsequent corrosion testing in 0.1 M NaCl
papers.findings: Both equal molar and Mg-rich compositions developed multiphase microstructures with intermetallic compounds (e.g., Ti2Zn, Mg21Zn25). A Ti-rich surface film (predominantly TiO2) forms during corrosion, leading to enhanced passivation and low corrosion current densities.
papers.mechanism: Processing-induced refinement and homogenization promote the formation of a passivating Ti-rich oxide film on the non-equilibrium microstructure, thereby reducing local galvanic couples and improving corrosion resistance.

papers.title: First principles-based design of lightweight high entropy alloys.
papers.system: Lightweight HEA families (e.g., AlBeMgTiSi, AlBeMgTiCu, AlBeMgTiLi)
papers.approach: High-throughput density functional theory (DFT) calculations and Grand Canonical Linear Programming to evaluate phase stability at 0 K and room temperature
papers.findings: Identified top compositions exhibiting negative formation energies and low densities while being metastable in the single solid-solution state; indicated that certain alloys (e.g., AlBeMgTiSi) are intrinsically stable while others require rapid cooling to freeze the non-equilibrium state.
papers.mechanism: The thermodynamic energy landscape, including contributions from configurational entropy, dictates the stability of the metastable single-phase state, influencing subsequent transformation pathways under processing and service conditions.

papers.title: Mechanistic understanding of speciated oxide growth in high entropy alloys.
papers.system: Equiatomic CoCrFeNiMn alloy (with additional Al in some cases)
papers.approach: Controlled oxidation experiments at low temperatures (around 400 °C) with in situ/ex situ TEM, atom probe tomography (APT), and X-ray absorption techniques
papers.findings: Oxidation leads to the rapid formation of layered oxide films, with sequential enrichment of Ni, followed by Cr-rich and then Fe/Co/Mn-rich layers. The process is accompanied by defect formation due to atomic diffusion and surface elasticity.
papers.mechanism: Selective oxidation driven by differences in redox potentials and atomic sizes results in a stratified oxide scale. Although not Mg-containing, the insights on layer formation and passivation mechanisms are transferable to systems where non-equilibrium phase evolution influences oxidation behavior.

papers.title: Characterisation of a Novel Complex Concentrated Alloy for Marine Applications.
papers.system: Al–Cu–Si–Zn–Mg alloy designed for low density (≈2.63 g/cm³)
papers.approach: Melt casting followed by heat treatment, with microstructural characterization (SEM, XRD) and corrosion testing in marine-simulated environments
papers.findings: Exhibited a dendritic primary α-Al matrix reinforced with intermetallic phases (notably Al2Cu) and demonstrated significantly lower corrosion rates (up to six times slower) than conventional steels.
papers.mechanism: The controlled spatial distribution and fine dispersion of intermetallic compounds within a lightweight matrix contribute to enhanced passivation and improved high-temperature oxidation resistance.

established: Non-equilibrium processing of lightweight alloys leads to metastable solid solution states that subsequently evolve via diffusion-driven precipitation into a mixture of solid solutions and intermetallic compounds.
Mg-containing lightweight HEAs and CCAs achieve low densities (<6 g/cm³) while often exhibiting complex multiphase microstructures.
Passivation (via formation of Ti-rich or other protective oxide films) is a key mechanism in enhancing corrosion and high-temperature oxidation resistance.

Processing techniques such as rapid cooling, mechanical alloying (ball milling), and spark plasma sintering are effective in retaining non-equilibrium phases that later transform under thermal exposure.

approaches_tried.approach: CALPHAD, kinetic and diffusion simulations combined with heat treatment
approaches_tried.outcome: Successful identification of multiphase structures and prediction of invariant transformations; some differences noted versus experimental phase compositions.

approaches_tried.approach: High-energy ball milling and spark plasma sintering
approaches_tried.outcome: Production of refined microstructures with favorable corrosion resistance through formation of passivating Ti-rich surface films.
Identification of metastable lightweight HEA compositions with low formation energies that inform required processing strategies.

approaches_tried.approach: In situ oxidation studies using TEM, APT, and XANES
approaches_tried.outcome: Elucidated layer-by-layer oxidation mechanisms and provided a framework for understanding selective oxide growth in complex alloys.

mechanisms: Diffusion-driven precipitation from non-equilibrium solid solutions causing sequential intermetallic formation.
Formation of passivating surface films (e.g., Ti-rich oxides) via selective oxidation of alloying elements.
Elemental segregation controlled by kinetic limitations during rapid cooling or mechanical processing.
Selective oxidation influenced by atomic size, redox potential, and chemical interaction between multiple alloying species.
disagreements: Some simulation approaches (e.g., CALPHAD) overestimate the stability or quantity of certain predicted phases relative to experimental observations.
Variations exist in reported ordering and precipitation sequences, highlighting discrepancies between predictive models and observed microstructures.
The precise role of minor elemental differences (e.g., Mg content variations) in controlling passivation versus micro-galvanic corrosion remains debated.
open_questions: What are the detailed transformation pathways from the non-equilibrium (metastable) state to the final multiphase distribution in Mg-containing lightweight HEAs?
How does variation in Mg concentration specifically affect the evolution of protective oxide films during high-temperature oxidation?
Can controlled heat treatment regimes be developed to tailor the spatial distribution of intermetallic phases for optimized corrosion resistance?
How do processing parameters (e.g., cooling rate, mechanical alloying intensity) quantitatively influence the kinetics of phase transformation in these alloys?
opportunities: Combine rapid solidification or mechanical alloying (ball milling/SPS) with targeted heat treatment to control the transformation from a supersaturated solid solution to a tailored intermetallic dispersion.
Incorporate alloying elements (e.g., Ti, Zn) that facilitate the formation of stable, passivating oxide layers to counteract the inherent galvanic effects of Mg.
Utilize integrated computational-experimental approaches (CALPHAD + DFT + in situ oxidation studies) to better predict and validate transformation pathways.
Investigate compositionally graded or microstructurally heterogeneous samples to delineate the effect of local variations on corrosion and high-temperature oxidation behavior.
Develop in situ diagnostic methods during heat treatment and oxidation to capture real-time evolution of the non-equilibrium microstructure.

directions.direction: Thermal annealing to trigger diffusion‐driven precipitation in a non‐equilibrium cast alloy.
directions.assessment: Directly addresses the transformation pathway from a supersaturated solid solution to a multiphase microstructure. Well supported by diffusion‐driven precipitation observations (PMC7579168::web::035::5_conclusions, PMC9100001::web::023::4_conclusions) and is feasible using controlled annealing experiments. It is informative regarding both corrosion and high-temperature oxidation changes.

directions.direction: Isothermal treatment to induce localized segregation and intermetallic network formation.
directions.assessment: Attacks the mechanism by which non‐equilibrium segregation changes local composition. Supports hypotheses on selective sites for oxide nucleation and subsequent barrier formation, as observed in related Al–Mg systems (PMC7579168::web::000::abstract, PMC10728166::web::052::energetical_stability).

directions.direction: Mechanical alloying (ball milling + SPS) followed by controlled aging to produce a nanocrystalline metastable state with grain-boundary precipitates.
directions.assessment: This route exploits non‐equilibrium processing to create a fine microstructure. Evidence shows that processing-induced refinement can enhance passivation and lower corrosion (PMC12299034::web::035::4_conclusions, PMC12299034::web::007::1_introduction); it directly targets the evolution mechanism and its effect on oxidation and corrosion.

directions.direction: Directional solidification to create a compositional and microstructural gradient in the alloy.
directions.assessment: By introducing a graded microstructure, this intervention probes how spatial variations in intermetallic phase density influence oxidation and corrosion. Prior studies on compositionally graded alloys (e.g., MgAlCuZnGd) and microstructural effects support this approach (PMC9102090::web::026::5_conclusions, PMC9102090::web::004::1_introduction).

candidates.hypothesis: Controlled moderate-temperature annealing of a rapidly solidified, non-equilibrium MgAlCuZnGd lightweight HEA will induce diffusion-driven precipitation of fine-scale Mg2Si (and similar) intermetallic phases that reduce local galvanic coupling, thus promoting the formation of a continuous, protective oxide layer during high-temperature exposure, resulting in lower corrosion current density and enhanced oxidation resistance.
candidates.intervention: Anneal the as-cast alloy at approximately 350°C for 2 hours.

candidates.hypothesis: Isothermal treatment of a non-equilibrium MgAlCuZnGd alloy at 400°C will drive localized elemental segregation that forms a discrete intermetallic network at sub-micron length scales, which acts as preferential oxide nucleation sites and barriers to corrosive attack, thereby improving both high-temperature oxidation resistance and reducing corrosion rates relative to a homogeneous microstructure.
candidates.intervention: Hold the alloy isothermally at 400°C for 90 minutes.

candidates.hypothesis: A nanocrystalline Mg-containing HEA produced via high-energy ball milling followed by spark plasma sintering, when subjected to a mild aging treatment at 300°C for 1 hour, will develop coherent grain-boundary intermetallic precipitates that block intergranular corrosion pathways and provide preferential sites for forming a dense, protective oxide film during high-temperature exposure, thus enhancing both corrosion and oxidation resistance.
candidates.intervention: Post-consolidation aging at 300°C for 1 hour in an inert atmosphere.

candidates.hypothesis: Introducing a directional solidification process to create a compositional gradient in a MgAlCuZnGd HEA will result in an outer region with a higher volume fraction of fine intermetallic precipitates, which in turn acts as a scaffold for forming a denser, passivating oxide film during high-temperature exposure and reduces overall corrosion rates compared to a uniformly processed alloy.
candidates.intervention: Directional solidification to intentionally create a compositional/microstructural gradient across the sample.
